Figure 13: Percent Change in Drying Rate and Energy Intensity vs. Dry Basis Moisture Content for a 300 GSM SW Bl 800 W RF+Base Trial The above experiments were repeated with other basis weights and process conditions including varying RF power levels. The results showed that RF drying is indeed an effective method for paper drying applications with greater improvements in drying rates and energy intensities at higher moisture contents. At lower moisture contents, RF is ineffective as a drying method even though the volumetric drying can be used to even out local variations in moisture content profiles (Grassmann 1980). RF drying is especially effective at higher basis weights, as in packaging grades, which are in general more difficult to dry using the current commercial technologies. This analysis complemented theoretical studies on RF’s effects in drying systems. The results demonstrated improvements in drying rate and energy efficiency across a range of RF power levels, paper types, basis weights, and drying approaches, with high repeatability, ensuring a solid foundation for future studies in drying process improvements and simulation-based modeling. US Energy Applications Similar to the RF work, the application of US energy in conjunction with conduction and convection drying was explored in the contact application mode. Here two cycles of conduction and convection drying with 150 C hot plate and 100 C heated air at 5 m/s velocity which was followed by 5 s of US application – 28 kilohertz (kHz) and 120 W. Above was repeated 5 times until the sheet was relatively dry and then completed with base case conduction and convection. Similar experiments were conducted at other US frequencies. The average drying rates obtained during the 5s of US applications were compared with the average drying rates during the prior combined conduction and convection cycle (base case) for each application. These comparisons showed that the US applications did not result in an appreciable increase in drying rates. It is 22 DE-EE0009395 interesting that for all three basis weights the above regimen of application did not result in any appreciable increase in drying rate improvements or energy intensity improvements when compared to the base case conduction and convection cycles. This could be due to the base case conduction and convection cycles taken together already provided a good drying rate and US application was not effective in providing additional water removal. On the other hand, when the above data was compared in an alternate manner, with the US performance compared with only the prior convection portion of the overall drying process, i.e. similar to what will be present in the pockets, we did see relatively better improvements in drying rate and energy intensity.
